claim: A small, nucleotide-binding domain, the ATP-cone, is found at the N-terminus of most ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) catalytic subunits.
source: A small, nucleotide-binding domain, the ATP-cone, is found at the N-terminus of most ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) catalytic subunits.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about RNR structure, supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: The ATP-cone regulates enzyme activity of all classes of RNR by binding adenosine triphosphate (ATP) or deoxyadenosine triphosphate (dATP).
source: By binding adenosine triphosphate (ATP) or deoxyadenosine triphosphate (dATP) it regulates the enzyme activity of all classes of RNR.
evidence: This is a general statement about RNR regulation supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: dATP inhibits activity of aerobic RNRs by inducing oligomerisation and preventing productive radical transfer from one subunit to the active site in the other.
source: Functional and structural work on aerobic RNRs has revealed a plethora of ways in which dATP inhibits activity by inducing oligomerisation and preventing a productive radical transfer from one subunit to the active site in the other.
evidence: This statement references prior functional and structural work on aerobic RNRs, indicating citation-based support.

claim: Anaerobic RNRs store a stable glycyl radical next to the active site.
source: Anaerobic RNRs, on the other hand, store a stable glycyl radical next to the active site and the basis for their dATP-dependent inhibition is completely unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge about anaerobic RNR structure.

claim: The basis for dATP-dependent inhibition in anaerobic RNRs was completely unknown prior to this study.
source: Anaerobic RNRs, on the other hand, store a stable glycyl radical next to the active site and the basis for their dATP-dependent inhibition is completely unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The anaerobic RNR from Prevotella copri exists in a dimer-tetramer equilibrium biased towards dimers when two ATP molecules are bound to the ATP-cone.
source: The enzyme exists in a dimer–tetramer equilibrium biased towards dimers when two ATP molecules are bound to the ATP-cone and tetramers when two dATP molecules are bound.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the GEMMA experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The anaerobic RNR from Prevotella copri exists in a dimer-tetramer equilibrium biased towards tetramers when two dATP molecules are bound to the ATP-cone.
source: The enzyme exists in a dimer–tetramer equilibrium biased towards dimers when two ATP molecules are bound to the ATP-cone and tetramers when two dATP molecules are bound.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the GEMMA experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the presence of ATP, P. copri NrdD is active and has a fully ordered glycyl radical domain (GRD) in one monomer of the dimer.
source: In the presence of ATP, P. copri NrdD is active and has a fully ordered glycyl radical domain (GRD) in one monomer of the dimer.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cryo-EM structures and activity assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Binding of dATP to the ATP-cone results in loss of activity and increased dynamics of the GRD, such that it cannot be detected in the cryo-EM structures.
source: Binding of dATP to the ATP-cone results in loss of activity and increased dynamics of the GRD, such that it cannot be detected in the cryo-EM structures.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cryo-EM structures and activity assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The glycyl radical is formed even in the dATP-bound form of P. copri NrdD.
source: The glycyl radical is formed even in the dATP-bound form, but the substrate does not bind.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EPR experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Substrate does not bind to the dATP-bound form of P. copri NrdD.
source: The glycyl radical is formed even in the dATP-bound form, but the substrate does not bind.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MST experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: dATP inhibition in anaerobic RNRs acts by increasing the flexibility of the flap and GRD, thereby preventing both substrate binding and radical mobilisation.
source: Taken together, the results suggest that dATP inhibition in anaerobic RNRs acts by increasing the flexibility of the flap and GRD, thereby preventing both substrate binding and radical mobilisation.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion inferred from the combined structural, biochemical, and biophysical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RNRs produce all four deoxyribonucleotides and are the only enzymes providing de novo building blocks for DNA replication and repair in all free-living organisms.
source: RNRs produce all four deoxyribonucleotides and are the only enzymes providing de novo building blocks for DNA replication and repair in all free-living organisms (Mathews, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mathews, 2016.

claim: Virtually all RNRs possess an allosteric site regulating substrate specificity (the s-site).
source: Virtually all RNRs possess an allosteric site regulating substrate specificity (the s-site), a crucial aspect of RNR that ultimately provides a balanced supply of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) (Mathews, 2016; Mathews, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mathews, 2016 and Mathews, 2018.

claim: The ATP-cone is found in the majority of RNRs.
source: A second allosteric site (the a-site) is located in an N-terminal domain called the ATP-cone (Aravind et al., 2000), found in the majority of RNRs (Jonna et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jonna et al., 2015.

claim: Binding of ATP activates RNR.
source: Binding of ATP activates RNR, and binding of dATP inhibits it (Hofer et al., 2012; Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hofer et al., 2012 and Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020.

claim: Binding of dATP inhibits RNR.
source: Binding of ATP activates RNR, and binding of dATP inhibits it (Hofer et al., 2012; Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hofer et al., 2012 and Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020.

claim: The RNR family consists of three evolutionarily related classes (I–III) with a common radical-based reaction mechanism but differing in the mode of radical generation and in quaternary structure.
source: The RNR family consists of three evolutionarily related classes (I–III) with a common radical-based reaction mechanism but differing in the mode of radical generation and in quaternary structure (Wiley, 2001; Lundin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wiley, 2001 and Lundin et al., 2015.

claim: Class I RNRs are strictly aerobic heterotetramers consisting of two α subunits (NrdA) with binding sites for substrates and allosteric nucleotides and two β subunits (NrdB) that harbour a radical initiator.
source: Class I, strictly aerobic RNRs are heterotetramers consisting of two α subunits (NrdA) with binding sites for substrates and allosteric nucleotides and two β subunits (NrdB) that harbour a radical initiator in the form of a stable radical or an oxidised metal cluster (Wiley, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wiley, 2001.

claim: Class III RNRs only function anaerobically.
source: Class III RNRs, which only function anaerobically, are dimers of an α subunit (NrdD) with a stable radical close to the active site, and binding sites for allosteric nucleotides.
evidence: This is established knowledge about class III RNRs.

claim: Class III RNRs are dimers of an α subunit (NrdD) with a stable radical close to the active site, and binding sites for allosteric nucleotides.
source: Class III RNRs, which only function anaerobically, are dimers of an α subunit (NrdD) with a stable radical close to the active site, and binding sites for allosteric nucleotides.
evidence: This is established knowledge about class III RNR structure.

claim: The radical in class III RNRs is introduced via encounter with a specific radical-SAM enzyme called NrdG.
source: The radical is introduced via encounter with a specific radical-SAM enzyme called NrdG, and once activated NrdD can perform multiple turnovers in the absence of NrdG (Backman et al., 2017; Torrents et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Backman et al., 2017 and Torrents et al., 2001.

claim: Once activated, NrdD can perform multiple turnovers in the absence of NrdG.
source: The radical is introduced via encounter with a specific radical-SAM enzyme called NrdG, and once activated NrdD can perform multiple turnovers in the absence of NrdG (Backman et al., 2017; Torrents et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Backman et al., 2017 and Torrents et al., 2001.

claim: A common denominator of all inhibited class I RNRs is oligomerisation, leading to disturbed radical transfer between the α and β subunits.
source: A common denominator of all inhibited class I RNRs is oligomerisation, leading to disturbed radical transfer between the α and β subunits.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from multiple cited studies on class I RNRs.

claim: Four different inhibitory oligomerisation mechanisms have been identified in class I RNRs: heterooctameric α4β4 complexes in Escherichia coli, Clostridium botulinum, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
source: Hitherto four different inhibitory oligomerisation mechanisms have been identified: heterooctameric α4β4 complexes in Escherichia coli, Clostridium botulinum, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ando et al., 2011; Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2014), an α4 complex in Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Johansson et al., 2016), α6 complexes in the eukaryotes Homo sapiens, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and Dictyostelium discoideum (Ando et al., 2016; Brignole et al., 2018; Crona et al., 2013; Fairman et al., 2011), and a β4 complex in the bacterium Leeuwenhoekiella blandensis (Rozman Grinberg et al., 2018a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ando et al., 2011; Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020; and Wei et al., 2014.

claim: An α4 complex forms in Pseudomonas aeruginosa class I RNR upon dATP inhibition.
source: Hitherto four different inhibitory oligomerisation mechanisms have been identified: heterooctameric α4β4 complexes in Escherichia coli, Clostridium botulinum, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ando et al., 2011; Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2014), an α4 complex in Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Johansson et al., 2016), α6 complexes in the eukaryotes Homo sapiens, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and Dictyostelium discoideum (Ando et al., 2016; Brignole et al., 2018; Crona et al., 2013; Fairman et al., 2011), and a β4 complex in the bacterium Leeuwenhoekiella blandensis (Rozman Grinberg et al., 2018a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Johansson et al., 2016.

claim: α6 complexes form in the eukaryotes Homo sapiens, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and Dictyostelium discoideum class I RNRs upon dATP inhibition.
source: Hitherto four different inhibitory oligomerisation mechanisms have been identified: heterooctameric α4β4 complexes in Escherichia coli, Clostridium botulinum, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ando et al., 2011; Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2014), an α4 complex in Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Johansson et al., 2016), α6 complexes in the eukaryotes Homo sapiens, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and Dictyostelium discoideum (Ando et al., 2016; Brignole et al., 2018; Crona et al., 2013; Fairman et al., 2011), and a β4 complex in the bacterium Leeuwenhoekiella blandensis (Rozman Grinberg et al., 2018a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ando et al., 2016; Brignole et al., 2018; Crona et al., 2013; and Fairman et al., 2011.

claim: A β4 complex forms in the bacterium Leeuwenhoekiella blandensis class I RNR upon dATP inhibition.
source: Hitherto four different inhibitory oligomerisation mechanisms have been identified: heterooctameric α4β4 complexes in Escherichia coli, Clostridium botulinum, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ando et al., 2011; Martínez-Carranza et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2014), an α4 complex in Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Johansson et al., 2016), α6 complexes in the eukaryotes Homo sapiens, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and Dictyostelium discoideum (Ando et al., 2016; Brignole et al., 2018; Crona et al., 2013; Fairman et al., 2011), and a β4 complex in the bacterium Leeuwenhoekiella blandensis (Rozman Grinberg et al., 2018a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rozman Grinberg et al., 2018a.

claim: All class I oligomers formed upon dATP inhibition involve protein–protein interactions mediated by the ATP-cone domain.
source: All of these class I oligomers involve protein–protein interactions mediated by the ATP-cone domain.
evidence: This statement summarizes a common feature of the cited class I RNR structures.

claim: The ATP-cone is found in about 80% of class III enzymes.
source: Among RNRs it is found in about 80% of class III enzymes and about 50% of class I enzymes, but less than 10% of class II enzymes (Jonna et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jonna et al., 2015.

claim: The ATP-cone is found in about 50% of class I enzymes.
source: Among RNRs it is found in about 80% of class III enzymes and about 50% of class I enzymes, but less than 10% of class II enzymes (Jonna et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jonna et al., 2015.

claim: The ATP-cone is found in less than 10% of class II enzymes.
source: Among RNRs it is found in about 80% of class III enzymes and about 50% of class I enzymes, but less than 10% of class II enzymes (Jonna et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jonna et al., 2015.

claim: The presence and function of the ATP-cone domain distinguish anaerobic RNRs from the other members of the large glycyl radical enzyme (GRE) family.
source: The presence and function of the ATP-cone domain distinguish anaerobic RNRs from the other members of the large glycyl radical enzyme (GRE) family that are otherwise structurally related (Backman et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Backman et al., 2017.

claim: The allosteric regulation mechanisms of class III RNRs from E. coli, bacteriophage T4 and Lactococcus lactis were determined several decades ago.
source: The allosteric regulation mechanisms of class III RNRs (NrdDs) from E. coli, bacteriophage T4 and Lactococcus lactis were determined several decades ago (Andersson et al., 2000; Eliasson et al., 1994; Torrents et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Andersson et al., 2000; Eliasson et al., 1994; and Torrents et al., 2000.

claim: T4NrdD was the first class III RNR structure solved.
source: T4NrdD was the first class III RNR structure solved (Logan et al., 1999), and later, structures of Thermotoga maritima NrdD (TmNrdD) have been published (Aurelius et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Logan et al., 1999.

claim: Structures of Thermotoga maritima NrdD have been published.
source: T4NrdD was the first class III RNR structure solved (Logan et al., 1999), and later, structures of Thermotoga maritima NrdD (TmNrdD) have been published (Aurelius et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Aurelius et al., 2015 and Wei et al., 2014.

claim: T4NrdD and TmNrdD lack an ATP-cone.
source: However, these two NrdDs lack an ATP-cone and the structural basis for allosteric activity regulation in the class III RNRs is still an outstanding question.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge of the published structures of these proteins.

claim: The structural basis for allosteric activity regulation in class III RNRs was an outstanding question prior to this study.
source: However, these two NrdDs lack an ATP-cone and the structural basis for allosteric activity regulation in the class III RNRs is still an outstanding question.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The final outcome of dATP inhibition is blocked radical transfer in both class I and III RNRs.
source: The final outcome of dATP inhibition is thus blocked radical transfer in both class I and III RNRs, but it is achieved by completely different mechanisms, i.e. oligomerisation prevents radical transfer between subunits in class I RNRs but long-range modulation of the flexibility of key structural elements prevents substrate binding in class III RNRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the combined data and comparison with class I RNRs.

claim: Oligomerisation prevents radical transfer between subunits in class I RNRs.
source: The final outcome of dATP inhibition is thus blocked radical transfer in both class I and III RNRs, but it is achieved by completely different mechanisms, i.e. oligomerisation prevents radical transfer between subunits in class I RNRs but long-range modulation of the flexibility of key structural elements prevents substrate binding in class III RNRs.
evidence: This statement summarizes the mechanism of dATP inhibition in class I RNRs based on cited literature.

claim: Long-range modulation of the flexibility of key structural elements prevents substrate binding in class III RNRs.
source: The final outcome of dATP inhibition is thus blocked radical transfer in both class I and III RNRs, but it is achieved by completely different mechanisms, i.e. oligomerisation prevents radical transfer between subunits in class I RNRs but long-range modulation of the flexibility of key structural elements prevents substrate binding in class III RNRs.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, inferred from the combined structural and biochemical data.

claim: PcNrdD belongs to the formate-requiring class III RNRs.
source: The amino acid sequence of PcNrdD suggests that it belongs to the formate-requiring class III RNRs (Burnim et al., 2022b; Wei et al., 2014), and initial optimisation of the assay composition showed that this was the case (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by sequence analysis (citation) and experimental data (figure reference).

claim: In the absence of any a-site effector, the basal level of GTP reduction by PcNrdD was 21 ± 2 nmol/min/mg.
source: With guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as substrate the s-site was filled with dTTP as effector, and in absence of any a-site effector the basal level of GTP reduction was 21 ± 2 nmol/min/mg.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the activity assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: An increasing concentration of ATP stimulated PcNrdD activity to a kcat of 1.3 s−1 (478 ± 26 nmol/min/mg), with a KL of 0.67 ± 0.12 mM.
source: An increasing concentration of ATP stimulated activity to a kcat of 1.3 s−1 (478 ± 26 nmol/min/mg), with a KL of 0.67 ± 0.12 mM (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the activity assays presented in Figure 1a.

claim: An increasing concentration of dATP resulted in an abrupt inhibition of PcNrdD enzyme activity with a Ki of 74 ± 24 µM.
source: On the other hand, an increasing concentration of dATP resulted in an abrupt inhibition of enzyme activity with a Ki of 74 ± 24 µM (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the activity assays presented in Figure 1b.

claim: The Ki value for dATP inhibition via the ATP-cone is approximately 10-fold lower compared to the KL value for ATP activation via the ATP-cone.
source: Hence, the Ki value for dATP inhibition via the ATP-cone is approximately 10-fold lower compared to the KL value for ATP activation via the ATP-cone.
evidence: This is a comparison of the measured Ki and KL values from the activity assays.

claim: Binding of dATP to PcNrdD occurred with a KD of 6 µM as measured by ITC.
source: Binding of dATP occurred with a KD of 6 µM, whereas binding of ATP was fourfold weaker with a KD of 26 µM (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the ITC experiments presented in Figure 2.

claim: Binding of ATP to PcNrdD occurred with a KD of 26 µM as measured by ITC.
source: Binding of dATP occurred with a KD of 6 µM, whereas binding of ATP was fourfold weaker with a KD of 26 µM (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the ITC experiments presented in Figure 2.

claim: Nucleotide binding measured with MST confirmed a KD of 25 µM for ATP binding to PcNrdD.
source: Nucleotide binding measured with MST confirmed our results for ATP (Figure 2d) that had a KD of 25 µM, and dATP that with this method had a KD of 23 µM (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the MST experiments presented in Figure 2d.

claim: Nucleotide binding measured with MST showed a KD of 23 µM for dATP binding to PcNrdD.
source: Nucleotide binding measured with MST confirmed our results for ATP (Figure 2d) that had a KD of 25 µM, and dATP that with this method had a KD of 23 µM (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the MST experiments presented in Figure 2e.

claim: The ATP-cone in PcNrdD can bind two ATP or two dATP molecules.
source: However, in cryo-EM experiments, where higher nucleotide concentrations can be used, we show that the ATP-cone can bind two ATP or two dATP molecules (see below), as also expected based on its sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cryo-EM structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only dATP was bound to PcNrdD when the protein was incubated with a combination of ATP and dATP.
source: Table 1 shows that only dATP was bound when PcNrdD was incubated with a combination of ATP and dATP.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the HPLC analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: The PcNrdD ATP-cone can bind either ATP or dATP but not both simultaneously.
source: In conclusion, the binding experiments suggest that the PcNrdD ATP-cone can bind either ATP or dATP but not both simultaneously.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the HPLC analysis of nucleotide binding presented in Table 1.

claim: There is allosteric communication between the s-site, the active site, and the a-site in the ATP-cone of PcNrdD.
source: Importantly, the results point to allosteric communication between the s-site, the active site, and the a-site in the ATP-cone, as dTTP and GTP are required for any ATP to be retained.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that s-site effector and substrate are required for ATP retention.

claim: When loaded with ATP, PcNrdD was in a dimer–tetramer equilibrium shifted towards dimers.
source: When loaded with ATP, PcNrdD was in a dimer–tetramer equilibrium shifted towards dimers (Figure 3a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the GEMMA experiments presented in Figure 3a and Table 2.

claim: The dimer–tetramer equilibrium of dATP-loaded PcNrdD was shifted towards tetramers.
source: In contrast, the dimer–tetramer equilibrium of dATP-loaded PcNrdD was shifted towards tetramers, and this equilibrium was likewise not affected by addition of the CTP substrate (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the GEMMA experiments presented in Figure 3b and Table 2.

claim: The glycyl radical was readily formed in the presence of dATP both with and without the CTP substrate.
source: Figure 4 shows that the glycyl radical was readily formed in the presence of dATP both with and without the CTP substrate, and the result was similar in the absence of formate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the EPR experiments presented in Figure 4.

claim: Under all conditions, the glycyl radical content was higher in the presence of dATP compared to with ATP.
source: Interestingly, under all conditions the glycyl radical content was higher in the presence of dATP compared to with ATP, and it was also more stable than in the absence of any effector nucleotides.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the EPR experiments presented in Figure 4.

claim: The glycyl radical was more stable in the presence of dATP than in the absence of any effector nucleotides.
source: Interestingly, under all conditions the glycyl radical content was higher in the presence of dATP compared to with ATP, and it was also more stable than in the absence of any effector nucleotides.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the EPR experiments presented in Figure 4.

claim: ATP-loaded PcNrdD bound GTP in the presence of s-site effector dTTP.
source: ATP-loaded PcNrdD bound GTP in the presence of s-site effector dTTP (Figure 5a), and it bound CTP in the presence of only ATP (Figure 5b), whereas dATP-loaded PcNrdD had extremely low affinity to GTP and CTP under similar conditions (Figure 5c, d).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the MST experiments presented in Figure 5a.

claim: ATP-loaded PcNrdD bound CTP in the presence of only ATP.
source: ATP-loaded PcNrdD bound GTP in the presence of s-site effector dTTP (Figure 5a), and it bound CTP in the presence of only ATP (Figure 5b), whereas dATP-loaded PcNrdD had extremely low affinity to GTP and CTP under similar conditions (Figure 5c, d).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the MST experiments presented in Figure 5b.

claim: dATP-loaded PcNrdD had extremely low affinity to GTP and CTP.
source: ATP-loaded PcNrdD bound GTP in the presence of s-site effector dTTP (Figure 5a), and it bound CTP in the presence of only ATP (Figure 5b), whereas dATP-loaded PcNrdD had extremely low affinity to GTP and CTP under similar conditions (Figure 5c, d).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the MST experiments presented in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: The dATP inhibition of enzyme activity in a class III RNR is mediated by inhibited binding of substrate.
source: These results show that the dATP inhibition of enzyme activity in a class III RNR is mediated by inhibited binding of substrate.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the MST substrate binding experiments presented in Figure 5.

claim: PcNrdD consists of 739 residues.
source: Each monomer consists of 739 residues, of which residues 1–91 constitute the ATP-cone, 92–110 a linker region, 111–122 a flap that folds over the substrate in the active site, 123–671 are the core domain with its 10-stranded α/β barrel fold typical of the RNR/GRE family, and 676–739 are the C-terminal glycyl radical domain (GRD) that contains a structural Zn2+ site followed by the buried loop containing the radical glycine residue at position Gly711 and a C-terminal tail that extends across the surface of the protein (Figure 6b, c).
evidence: This is a description of the structure determined by cryo-EM.

claim: Residues 1–91 of PcNrdD constitute the ATP-cone.
source: Each monomer consists of 739 residues, of which residues 1–91 constitute the ATP-cone, 92–110 a linker region, 111–122 a flap that folds over the substrate in the active site, 123–671 are the core domain with its 10-stranded α/β barrel fold typical of the RNR/GRE family, and 676–739 are the C-terminal glycyl radical domain (GRD) that contains a structural Zn2+ site followed by the buried loop containing the radical glycine residue at position Gly711 and a C-terminal tail that extends across the surface of the protein (Figure 6b, c).

evidence: This is a description of the structure determined by cryo-EM.

claim: The closest structural neighbours to PcNrdD are the NrdDs from bacteriophage T4 and T. maritima.
source: The closest structural neighbours as identified by the DALI server (Holm, 2022) are the NrdDs from bacteriophage T4 (Logan et al., 1999) (1H7A, 2.5 Å root mean square deviation [rmsd] in Cα positions for 535 residues, 27% sequence identity) and T. maritima (Aurelius et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2014) (4U3E, 3.0 Å rmsd for 508 residues, 16% sequence identity; Table 3).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison using the DALI server.

claim: The linker, flap, and GRD are well-ordered in one of the monomers of the ATP–CTP complex and substrate CTP is bound.
source: The linker, flap, and GRD are well-ordered in one of the monomers (dark blue in Figure 6) and substrate CTP is bound (Figure 6e), while in the other monomer this region is less well-ordered and the active site is empty (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–CTP complex.

claim: In the other monomer of the ATP–CTP complex, the linker, flap, and GRD region is less well-ordered and the active site is empty.
source: The linker, flap, and GRD are well-ordered in one of the monomers (dark blue in Figure 6) and substrate CTP is bound (Figure 6e), while in the other monomer this region is less well-ordered and the active site is empty (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–CTP complex.

claim: At the concentration of ATP used (1 mM), ATP is not observed to bind to the s-sites near the dimer interface.
source: At the concentration of ATP used (1 mM), ATP is not observed to bind to the s-sites near the dimer interface.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–CTP complex.

claim: The ATP molecules in PcNrdD are bound similarly to the twin dATP molecules seen in the ATP-cones of P. aeruginosa NrdA and L. blandensis NrdB.
source: The ATP molecules are bound similarly to the twin dATP molecules seen in the ATP-cones of P. aeruginosa NrdA (PaNrdA) and L. blandensis NrdB (LbNrdB) (Johansson et al., 2016; Rozman Grinberg et al., 2018a), and to dATP bound to PcNrdD itself (see below).
evidence: This is a comparison of the PcNrdD structure with previously published structures.

claim: The ATP-cones in PcNrdD exhibit a hitherto unobserved relative orientation in which the four triphosphate groups are projected towards each other.
source: However, the ATP-cones in PcNrdD exhibit a hitherto unobserved relative orientation in which the four triphosphate groups are projected towards each other (Figure 6b, d).
evidence: This is a novel observation from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–CTP complex.

claim: The large negative charge of the four triphosphate groups in the ATP-cone dimer is compensated for by the proximity of as many as 12 Arg and Lys side chains from both monomers.
source: The large negative charge is compensated for by the proximity of as many as 12 Arg and Lys side chains from both monomers.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–CTP complex.

claim: The closest atom of any ATP molecule is over 30 Å from the substrate CTP in the active site.
source: However, the closest atom of any ATP molecule is over 30 Å from the substrate CTP in the active site.
evidence: This is a measurement from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–CTP complex.

claim: The glycyl radical site in PcNrdD is found at Gly711, at the tip of a loop projected from the C-terminal region of the enzyme into the barrel.
source: The glycyl radical site is found at Gly711, at the tip of a loop projected from the C-terminal region of the enzyme into the barrel, where it approaches the radical initiator cysteine Cys416 at the tip of a loop stretching through the barrel from the other side (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The radical initiator cysteine in PcNrdD is Cys416.
source: The glycyl radical site is found at Gly711, at the tip of a loop projected from the C-terminal region of the enzyme into the barrel, where it approaches the radical initiator cysteine Cys416 at the tip of a loop stretching through the barrel from the other side (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The second cysteine necessary for the radical mechanism of PcNrdD is Cys171 on the first β-strand of the barrel.
source: The second cysteine necessary for the radical mechanism of PcNrdD is Cys171 on the first β-strand of the barrel (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: PcNrdD belongs to the group of anaerobic RNRs that use formate as overall reductant.
source: Consistent with the fact that PcNrdD belongs to the group of anaerobic RNRs that use formate as overall reductant (Burnim et al., 2022a; Mulliez et al., 1995; Wei et al., 2014), there is no third cysteine residue on the sixth β-strand, and its place is taken by Asn435.
evidence: This is supported by the structure and citations to prior work.

claim: There is no third cysteine residue on the sixth β-strand of PcNrdD, and its place is taken by Asn435.
source: Consistent with the fact that PcNrdD belongs to the group of anaerobic RNRs that use formate as overall reductant (Burnim et al., 2022a; Mulliez et al., 1995; Wei et al., 2014), there is no third cysteine residue on the sixth β-strand, and its place is taken by Asn435.
evidence: This is a description of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Gly711 in PcNrdD is completely buried within the barrel, with no solvent-accessible surface area.
source: As usual for GREs, Gly711 is completely buried within the barrel, with no solvent-accessible surface area.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The NxN flap in PcNrdD corresponds to a disordered segment of 17 residues in the structures of TmNrdD and T4NrdD.
source: This is the first time such interactions have been observed in an NrdD, as the flap corresponds to a disordered segment of 17 residues in the structures of TmNrdD and T4NrdD.
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published structures.

claim: An AlphaFold2 model of TmNrdD suggests that the linker potentially has the same conformation in TmNrdD and possibly all other NrdDs, whether or not they have an ATP-cone.
source: However, an AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) model of TmNrdD (entry Q9WYL) suggests that this linker potentially has the same conformation in TmNrdD and possibly all other NrdDs, whether or not they have an ATP-cone.
evidence: This is based on an AlphaFold2 prediction.

claim: The NxN flap forms the nexus of a network of interactions between the substrate, the linker to the ATP-cone, the C-terminal GRD, and loop 2.
source: Significantly, the NxN flap forms the nexus of a network of interactions (Figure 7) between the substrate, the linker to the ATP-cone, the C-terminal GRD, and 'loop 2' (residues 304–311) that is responsible for communicating the substrate specificity signal from the s-site at the dimer interface to the active site (Aurelius et al., 2015; Larsson et al., 2001; Logan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure and comparison with prior work.

claim: Loop 2 (residues 304–311) is responsible for communicating the substrate specificity signal from the s-site at the dimer interface to the active site.
source: Significantly, the NxN flap forms the nexus of a network of interactions (Figure 7) between the substrate, the linker to the ATP-cone, the C-terminal GRD, and 'loop 2' (residues 304–311) that is responsible for communicating the substrate specificity signal from the s-site at the dimer interface to the active site (Aurelius et al., 2015; Larsson et al., 2001; Logan et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Tyr712 is highly conserved in the NrdD family.
source: Tyr712 is highly conserved in the NrdD family (Figures 6f and 7).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: A tunnel ~12 Å long leading from the surface of the protein to the active site exists in the ATP-bound form of PcNrdD, with a diameter of 5.6 Å at its narrowest point.
source: As the NxN flap appears to close off the top of the active site, we used the web server Caver Web v1.1 (Stourac et al., 2019) to analyse substrate access to the active site in the ATP-bound form, and identified a tunnel ~12 Å long leading from the surface of the protein to the active site that is 5.6 Å in diameter at its narrowest point (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In principle, a fresh substrate could diffuse into the active site of PcNrdD on each catalytic cycle through the identified tunnel.
source: Thus, in principle a fresh substrate could diffuse into the active site on each catalytic cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of the tunnel identified in the structure.

claim: In the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex, the ATP-cone region is very flexible.
source: The ATP-cone region is very flexible, but the last helix of the ATP-cone in the active monomer can be traced back to residue 85 (Figure 8a, b).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex.

claim: The ATP–dTTP–GTP complex suggests that there is one partially disordered ATP-cone and one highly flexible ATP-cone.
source: Taken together, this suggests that there is one partially disordered ATP-cone and one highly flexible in the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM structure and 2D classes of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex.

claim: In the active monomer of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex, the NxN flap and entire C-terminus are ordered.
source: In the active monomer, the NxN flap and entire C-terminus are ordered while in the inactive monomer, the entire assembly of linker and NxN flap up to residue 120 and the entire GRD are so flexible that they cannot be seen in the cryo-EM volumes.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex.

claim: In the inactive monomer of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex, the entire assembly of linker and NxN flap up to residue 120 and the entire GRD are so flexible that they cannot be seen in the cryo-EM volumes.
source: In the active monomer, the NxN flap and entire C-terminus are ordered while in the inactive monomer, the entire assembly of linker and NxN flap up to residue 120 and the entire GRD are so flexible that they cannot be seen in the cryo-EM volumes.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex.

claim: Binding of dTTP to the s-sites at the dimer interface induces two distinct conformations of loop 2 in the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex.
source: Intriguingly, binding of dTTP to the s-sites at the dimer interface induces two distinct conformations of loop 2 (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex.

claim: In the active monomer of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex, loop 2 is projected towards the network of interactions between NxN flap, GRD, and substrate.
source: In the active monomer, loop 2 is projected towards the aforementioned network of interactions between NxN flap, GRD, and substrate, packing against the flap, though no polar interactions are apparent.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex.

claim: Loop 2 in the active monomer makes extensive interactions with its equivalent in the inactive monomer, which forces the latter into a conformation where it would sterically clash with an ordered NxN flap.
source: However, loop 2 also makes extensive interactions with its equivalent in the inactive monomer, which forces the latter into a conformation where it would sterically clash with an ordered NxN flap (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the ATP–dTTP–GTP complex.

claim: In the dATP-bound dimer, the entire GRD is disordered in both monomers.
source: Strikingly, in contrast to the ATP complexes, the entire GRD is disordered in both monomers of the dATP-bound dimer (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound dimer.

claim: No structure is visible after residue 676 at the end of the last strand of the barrel in the dATP-bound dimer.
source: No structure is visible after residue 676 at the end of the last strand of the barrel.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound dimer.

claim: Inhibition by binding of dATP to the ATP-cone is coupled to disordering of the C-terminal domain.
source: This suggests that inhibition by binding of dATP to the ATP-cone is coupled to disordering of the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the GRD is disordered in the dATP-bound dimer.

claim: The NxN flap is disordered in the dATP-bound dimer.
source: The NxN flap that covers the top of the substrate in the ATP/CTP-bound form is also disordered, as are the ATP-cones themselves.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound dimer.

claim: The ATP-cones are disordered in the dATP-bound dimer.
source: The NxN flap that covers the top of the substrate in the ATP/CTP-bound form is also disordered, as are the ATP-cones themselves.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound dimer.

claim: The dATP-bound tetramer reveals an arrangement of two dimers in which the ATP-cones are all well-ordered and one ATP-cone from each pair mediates interactions between the dimers.
source: The tetramer reveals an arrangement of two dimers (chains A/B and C/D, respectively) in which the ATP-cones are all well-ordered and one ATP-cone from each pair mediates interactions between the dimers (Figure 9b).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound tetramer.

claim: The ATP-cones in the dATP-bound tetramer have an almost domain-swapped arrangement within each dimer relative to the core domains.
source: The ATP-cones have an almost domain-swapped arrangement within each dimer relative to the core domains.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound tetramer.

claim: The oligomeric arrangement of the dATP-bound tetramer has not previously been observed within the RNR family.
source: This oligomeric arrangement has not previously been observed within the RNR family.
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published RNR structures.

claim: The two dATP molecules bound to each ATP-cone in the dATP-bound tetramer bind very much as they do to the dATP-loaded ATP-cones of PaNrdA and LbNrdB.
source: The two dATP molecules bound to each ATP-cone do so very much as they do to the dATP-loaded ATP-cones of the RNR class I active site subunit from PaNrdA (PDB ID 5IM3) and the class I radical generating subunit from LbNrdB (5OLK) to which the PcNrdD ATP-cones have 29% and 33% sequence identity, respectively (Table 4).
evidence: This is a comparison of the PcNrdD structure with previously published structures.

claim: The two dATP molecules in the ATP-cone bind with their negatively charged triphosphate moieties oriented towards each other.
source: The two dATP molecules bind with their negatively charged triphosphate moieties oriented towards each other (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound tetramer.

claim: No Mg2+ ion is observed between the triphosphate tails in the dATP-bound tetramer, but this may be an artefact of the cryo-EM method.
source: No Mg2+ ion is observed between the triphosphate tails, but this may be an artefact of the cryo-EM method, as the PaNrdA and LbNrdB crystal structures suggest that this ion is necessary for charge neutralisation.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure and comparison with crystal structures.

claim: The pair of ATP-cones in the dATP-bound tetramer is highly asymmetrically positioned with respect to the twofold axis of its core dimer.
source: Remarkably, the pair of ATP-cones is highly asymmetrically positioned with respect to the twofold axis of its core dimer, being displaced as a rigid body towards the other dimer (Figure 9b).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound tetramer.

claim: All contacts between the two dimers of the tetramer are mediated by interactions between one of the ATP-cones in one dimer and one of the core domains of the other dimer.
source: Interestingly, all contacts between the two dimers of the tetramer are mediated by interactions between one of the ATP-cones in one dimer (B or D) and one of the core domains of the other dimer (C or A, respectively).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound tetramer.

claim: The amount of buried surface area between the two dimers of the tetramer is 717 Å2, or around 1% of the total surface area of each dimer.
source: The amount of buried surface area is small: 717 Å2, or around 1% of the total surface area of each dimer.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the cryo-EM structure of the dATP-bound tetramer.

claim: The monomer–monomer interactions within each dimer bury 11.7% of the total area.
source: For comparison, the monomer–monomer interactions within each dimer bury 11.7% of the total area.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Both dATP–CTP complexes (tetramer and dimer) were almost identical to those seen in the presence of dATP alone, and no CTP could be seen bound to the active site.
source: Both forms were almost identical to those seen in the presence of dATP alone, and no CTP could be seen bound to the active site (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structures of the dATP–CTP complexes.

claim: Substrate binding is dependent on ordering of the flap region by binding of ATP to the ATP-cone.
source: This strongly suggests that substrate binding is dependent on ordering of the flap region by binding of ATP to the ATP-cone.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that no CTP is bound in the dATP–CTP complexes.

claim: The apo form of PcNrdD shows high deuterium uptake over the entire ATP-cone, linker, and NxN flap, from residues 1 to 117.
source: The apo form shows high deuterium uptake over the entire ATP-cone, linker, and NxN flap, from residues 1 to 117 (Figure 10a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the HDX-MS experiments presented in Figure 10a.

claim: Analysis of differences in HDX uptake in the N-terminal region between the apo protein and the ATP or dATP complexes clearly validates binding of both nucleotides to the ATP-cone.
source: Analysis of differences in uptake in the N-terminal region between the apo protein and the ATP or dATP complexes clearly validates binding of both nucleotides to the ATP-cone (Figure 10b).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the HDX-MS experiments presented in Figure 10b.

claim: Peptides spanning residues 2–84 exhibit clear protection from HDX in both nucleotide-bound states.
source: Peptides spanning residues 2–84 exhibit clear protection from HDX in both nucleotide-bound states.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the HDX-MS experiments.

claim: The HDX-MS results show a high degree of deuterium uptake in the GRD in all forms, indicating a high degree of mobility.
source: The HDX-MS results show a high degree of deuterium uptake in the GRD in all forms, indicating a high degree of mobility.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the HDX-MS experiments.

claim: The GRD overall has B-factors higher than the core domain in the cryo-EM structures.
source: This is consistent with the cryo-EM structures, in which the GRD overall has B-factors higher than the core domain (though the glycyl-radical containing loop has similar B-factors to the core, being buried).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: A trend of increased dynamics for some C-terminal peptides in the GRD can be seen for the dATP–CTP state in HDX-MS.
source: From the HDX-MS data, it is clear that the GRD is highly dynamic, and while a trend of increased dynamics for some C-terminal peptides in the GRD can be seen for the dATP–CTP state, a detailed analysis is confounded by the limited time resolution and the complexity of the sample, which consists of a mixture of conformations.
evidence: This is an observation from the HDX-MS experiments.

claim: The results show a clear correlation between ATP or dATP binding to the ATP-cone and activity or inhibition, respectively.
source: Taken together, our results show a clear correlation between ATP or dATP binding to the ATP-cone and activity or inhibition, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the combined data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The dynamical transitions involve a previously uncharacterised but highly conserved structural element, the NxN flap, that folds over the substrate and acts as a structural bridge between the ATP-cone and the C-terminal GRD.
source: The dynamical transitions involve a previously uncharacterised but highly conserved structural element, the NxN flap, that folds over the substrate and furthermore acts as a structural bridge between the ATP-cone and the C-terminal GRD.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: An increase in dynamics of the NxN flap and GRD prevents substrate binding and transfer of the radical from the GRD to the substrate.
source: An increase in dynamics of these elements prevents substrate binding and thus transfer of the radical from the GRD to the substrate.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion inferred from the combined structural and biochemical data.

claim: A similar flap is formed over the top of the active site in the E. coli active complex, but it is formed by part of the C-terminal region of the separate radical generating subunit.
source: Interestingly, a similar flap is formed over the top of the active site in the E. coli active complex, but it is formed by part of the C-terminal region of the separate radical generating subunit (Kang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previously published structure, supported by a citation.

claim: A locking of the substrate in the active site appears to be a conserved feature of active class I and III RNRs.
source: Thus, a locking of the substrate in the active site appears to be a conserved feature of active class I and III RNRs.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the PcNrdD structure with the E. coli class I RNR structure.

claim: In class I RNR there is no tunnel allowing substrate access to the active site in the locked state.
source: However, in class I RNR there is no tunnel allowing substrate access to the active site in the locked state.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of class I RNR structures.

claim: Class I subunits dissociate on each catalytic cycle.
source: This is consistent with the fact that the class I subunits dissociate on each catalytic cycle, while in class III the glycyl radical can catalyse many substrate reductions before having to be regenerated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about class I RNR mechanism.

claim: In class III RNRs, the glycyl radical can catalyse many substrate reductions before having to be regenerated.
source: This is consistent with the fact that the class I subunits dissociate on each catalytic cycle, while in class III the glycyl radical can catalyse many substrate reductions before having to be regenerated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about class III RNR mechanism.
